steps: Root system consists of roots, usually growing below the ground; shoot system consists of the stem, leaves, buds, flowers and fruits, usually growing above the ground.
Roots anchor the plant in the soil and absorb water and mineral salts; the shoot supports the plant and carries out functions such as photosynthesis, transport and reproduction.
Roots generally do not have nodes, internodes or leaves; the stem of the shoot has nodes and internodes and bears leaves and buds.
items.finalAnswer: The root system anchors the plant and absorbs water and minerals, while the shoot system bears the above-ground parts and performs functions such as support, photosynthesis, transport and reproduction.

steps: Epidermal tissue forms the outer covering of a plant and protects it from injury and water loss.
Epidermal cells are usually closely packed; the epidermis may have a waxy cuticle and stomata for gas exchange and water loss.
Mesophyll tissue is present inside the leaf, between the upper and lower epidermis.
Mesophyll cells contain chloroplasts and carry out photosynthesis; spaces between some mesophyll cells also allow gas exchange.
items.finalAnswer: Epidermal tissue covers and protects the plant, while mesophyll tissue inside the leaf performs photosynthesis and allows gas exchange.

steps: Palisade mesophyll is found below the upper epidermis of the leaf.
Its cells are elongated and closely packed, and contain many chloroplasts; it is the main site of photosynthesis.
Spongy mesophyll is usually found below the palisade mesophyll, toward the lower epidermis.
Its cells are irregular and loosely arranged, with large air spaces between them; these spaces help in the exchange of gases.
Spongy mesophyll cells also contain chloroplasts and carry out photosynthesis.
items.finalAnswer: Palisade mesophyll has closely packed, chloroplast-rich cells for photosynthesis, while spongy mesophyll has loosely arranged cells and air spaces that aid gas exchange.

steps: In multicellular organisms, cells are organized into levels: cells, tissues, organs, organ systems and the organism.
Cells are the basic structural and functional units of an organism; specialized cells perform particular functions.
A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform a particular function.
An organ consists of different tissues working together to perform specific functions.
An organ system consists of organs working together to perform major functions of the body.
All organ systems work in coordination to maintain the life of the organism.
items.finalAnswer: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form organ systems; coordinated organ systems make up and maintain the multicellular organism.

steps: The tissue level is the level of organization in which similar cells work together to perform a particular function.
Plant tissues are groups of plant cells with a common structure and function; they are broadly classified as meristematic and permanent tissues.
Meristematic tissues consist of actively dividing cells and bring about plant growth.
Permanent tissues consist of mature cells that perform specific functions, such as protection, support, storage and transport.
Animal tissues are groups of specialized cells that work together to perform particular functions.
The main types of animal tissues are epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues.

Epithelial tissue covers body surfaces and lines cavities; connective tissue supports and connects body parts; muscular tissue contracts to produce movement; nervous tissue receives and transmits messages.
items.finalAnswer: The tissue level is a group of similar cells working together; plant tissues include meristematic and permanent tissues, while the main animal tissues are epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous.

steps: The wall of the stomach is made of epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues.
Epithelial tissue lines the stomach and contains glands that secrete gastric juice; mucus helps protect the lining from the acidic juice.
Connective tissue supports and binds the stomach tissues and contains blood vessels that supply them.
Muscular tissue in the stomach wall contracts to churn and mix food with gastric juice and move it through the digestive tract.
Nervous tissue controls and coordinates the activities of the stomach.
items.finalAnswer: In the stomach, epithelial tissue secretes gastric juice and protects the lining, connective tissue supports and supplies it, muscular tissue churns and moves food, and nervous tissue coordinates activity.

steps: The leaf is composed mainly of epidermal, mesophyll and vascular tissues.
The upper and lower epidermis protect the leaf; the cuticle helps reduce water loss, and stomata allow gas exchange.
Mesophyll tissue lies between the epidermal layers. Palisade mesophyll contains many chloroplasts and is the main site of photosynthesis.
Spongy mesophyll has air spaces that allow gases to move through the leaf; its cells also carry out photosynthesis.
Vascular tissue occurs in the veins of the leaf. Xylem transports water and mineral salts to the leaf, while phloem transports the food made in the leaf to other parts of the plant.
items.finalAnswer: Epidermal tissue protects the leaf and enables gas exchange, mesophyll carries out photosynthesis, and vascular tissue transports water, minerals and food.

steps: The human body is organized into cells, tissues, organs and organ systems.
Different tissues combine to form organs, and organs that work together form an organ system.
The organ systems perform different functions but work in coordination with one another.
For example, the digestive system breaks down food and absorbs nutrients, the respiratory system supplies oxygen, and the circulatory system transports oxygen and nutrients to body cells.
Together, the organ systems maintain the activities and life of the human body.
items.finalAnswer: Different organs form organ systems, and the coordinated work of all organ systems performs the functions needed to maintain the human body.
